title: Close the three gaps between shipping a commit and verifying what actually got served

history.detail:
PASS: PASS — round 1. Audited 3829429, main checkout. Sprint file read fresh.

Two documented decisions get reversed here and a third precedent gets challenged head-on. All three survive the check. No FAIL.

================================================================
REQ 1 — GATE RELAXATION, DEMONSTRATED BOTH DIRECTIONS IN A SCRATCH REPO
================================================================

The criterion says reading the diff does not clear this, and a real code difference slipping through is a FAIL. Built a scratch repo, took a sprint through to a recorded ship, then landed a change and tried to record a live test against it. Seven cases:

    bookkeeping only (state/registry churn)     ACCEPTED   (intended relaxation)
    sprint file edited                          ACCEPTED   (intended relaxation)
    identical content, different SHA            ACCEPTED   (intended relaxation)
    one-line change to sprint_lifecycle.py      REFUSED
    launcher/run-role.js changed                REFUSED
    package.json version bumped                 REFUSED
    a brand-new scripts/backdoor.js             REFUSED
No real code difference slips through, including a file that did not exist at ship time.

THE MISMATCH MESSAGE NAMES THE PATHS, verified by producing one rather than reading the format string:
    "...doesn't match what Pipeman actually shipped (...), and it's not just bookkeeping — differs in:
     scripts/launcher/run-role.js, scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py. Re-test against what was actually
     deployed... No override."
Both changed paths named. And the helper was reused, not reimplemented — `git_tree_hash_excluding` and `SHIP_HASH_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS` are sprint 13's own, with `differing_paths_excluding()` added alongside for the naming and documented as dropping the same patterns the hash does.

ON REVERSING SPRINT 7's DELIBERATE CHOICE, since this is the second documented decision this sprint overturns: cmd_liveqa's identity check was deliberate, and its old comment said so — "there's no legitimate rebase/squash step between shipping and deploying that would need tolerating here." That reasoning was about the *deploy* step, and it is still true for a deployed web app. What changed underneath it is that this project's own releases now routinely put bookkeeping commits between ship and verify, which is exactly the class sprint 13 already excluded from the ship gate for the same reason. Applying the same exclusion to the same class at the next gate is consistent rather than a loosening — and the seven probes above are what makes that a checked claim rather than an argued one.

Worth crediting: Dev Team found that this change silently broke an existing smoke test, because the old "mismatched deployed-commit" case used an `--allow-empty` commit — content-identical to its parent, so correctly ACCEPTED under the new rules, leaving a test that would have kept passing while testing nothing. Fixed to use a real content change. That is the failure mode a relaxation actually produces, and it was caught by running the suite rather than by reading it.

================================================================
REQ 3 — I PUSHED ON THE PRECEDENT ARGUMENT, AS ASKED. IT HOLDS.
================================================================

Dev Team flagged this as the thing to check rather than take on their word, which was the right call — it directly contradicts a ruling I audited in sprint 7.

The argument: `worktree_divergence_warning()` answered "does another location have a DIFFERENT sprint file", a two-directional question where a stale ref reads as agreement when the truth is unknown — genuine false confidence. This function answers only "does origin contain at least one commit beyond `last_shipped_commit`", monotonic and one-directional, so under append-only history a stale local view can only see FEWER of origin's commits, never invent ones that are not there. Staleness under-reports; it cannot raise a false alarm.

I tried to break it:
  - Does it ever assert the reassuring direction? No. Every path returns None or a warning string —
    silence when there is nothing to report, never "you are up to date," which is the claim staleness
    would actually falsify. That is the property the whole argument rests on and it holds in the code.
  - Does a force-push break the monotonic assumption? It could remove commits from origin, but that
    still only makes the check see fewer, and any commit it does see beyond the record genuinely is
    beyond the record. No false alarm either way.
  - Does it reintroduce the network dependency sprint 7 cared about? No — it does not fetch, and says
    so, preserving the local-and-enumerable property that ruling was also protecting.
  - Every ambiguous case (no upstream, detached HEAD, unresolvable ref, not a repo, no shipped commit)
    returns None rather than guessing.
The distinction is real and the sprint 7 ruling still correctly stands for its own check. Addressing the precedent in the docstring rather than citing a different Req number past it is the right way to do this, and it is the reason I could check it at all.

WARNS, NEVER GATES — verified by construction: no `die`, no `sys.exit`, on any path.

READ COLD, the message forecloses the exact misreading the criterion names: "This means the remote and this record have drifted apart — it does NOT mean someone bypassed the push-only-Pipeman rule," followed by the likely real cause (a second real ship landing before its own bookkeeping caught up). It also surfaces the staleness caveat where the reader actually is, not only in the docstring: "a stale local view under-reports this, it never over-reports it."

================================================================
REQ 2 — THE SPECIFICITY IS REAL
================================================================

The criterion's defect condition is a check satisfied by "a run exists" or "a run completed." It is not. Red concludes refuse; and for a run that concluded success, it inspects the jobs and requires that a step other than GitHub's own injected ones actually executed — "Set up job", "Complete job", and any "Post *" are excluded by name. The comment records why, and it is the bug Dev Team's own smoke test caught in their first draft: "Set up job" alone already satisfies a naive check, on exactly the case the check exists to catch. A run that exited EUSAGE at install in five seconds concludes failure and is refused; a run that succeeded with nothing but synthetic steps is refused by the second half.

THE UNDETERMINABLE DECISION IS RECORDED WITH ITS REASONING and behaves as the criterion requires — warns and proceeds, so a project with no CI configured is not silently unshippable. The no-runs-found case is explicitly folded in there rather than treated as red.

Not verified end to end against a real GitHub Actions run — correctly stated as such, and consistent with this project's established pattern for external dependencies (the fake `gh` matches `withFakeClaude`'s shape). Given sprint 26's finding, a live run would in any case only have told us about one execution.

REQ 4 / REQ 5 — package.json 0.1.25, the slot sprint 26 reserved. Ran the suites: ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED; ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED, 181 OK; verify-tarball.sh PASSED, "Installed 0.1.25 (first install)". Confirmed the five named cases exist as their own smoke sections rather than trusting the handoff: red CI refuses, succeeded-but-no-real-step refuses, undeterminable warns without gating, genuinely green ships, origin-ahead warns in both status and liveqa without gating, plus a silent-when-nothing-to-report case and the Req 1 bookkeeping-accepted case.

INFORMATIONAL

1. cmd_reship deliberately does not get the CI check, on the stated grounds that Req 2 names only
   /sprint-ship. That is the correct reading of the requirement and the right instinct not to add
   friction unasked — but it is worth Master Controller knowing the gap exists on purpose: a reship
   pushes a commit gate 1 has never seen, which is arguably where a CI check earns more, not less.
   A decision to make deliberately rather than inherit.
2. Carried, unchanged: every allowlist entry other than git and npm remains inferred; the empty-string
   ownedRepository declaration still falls through silently.

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it. /sprint-dev-done 24, then Pipeman ships and publishes 0.1.25, then `verify-publish 24`.

Note for Pipeman specifically: this is the first release where /sprint-ship itself can refuse on CI status. If it refuses, that is the new check working — read which of the two conditions it names (concluded not-success, or succeeded with no real step) before treating it as a tooling problem.

CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL — round 2. Audited bdd74bc, main checkout. Sprint file read fresh from the committed copy — which is the point of this round and the reason it is not the short one it was described as.

MY ROUND-1 HOLD IS RESOLVED. The sprint file is tracked in 2-in-progress, sprint-24.json is in git for the first time, and registry.json is committed. The index to the record and the record itself are both durable now. The answer on sprint 25/27 and the registry — same drift, not work in progress — is what I suspected and it is better to have it stated than inferred.

================================================================
THE FINDING — A NEW REQUIREMENT LANDED IN THE SPEC WITHOUT ITS IMPLEMENTATION
================================================================

This round was handed to me as "the short diff it promised": one line, package.json, 0.1.25 to 0.1.28. The code diff is exactly that — I confirmed `git diff 3829429 HEAD -- scripts/ .claude/ package.json` is package.json alone, one insertion, one deletion.

The spec is not. Diffing the committed spec against the copy I audited at round 1 shows the version renumbering AND a new requirement:

  4. **`cmd_reship` gets the same CI check as `cmd_ship`.** *Added mid-flight, on QA1's carried
     question, while a re-audit was already required for the version renumbering.*
with its own acceptance criterion:
  - Req 4: confirm `cmd_reship` uses the same check and the same undeterminable-status behaviour as
    `cmd_ship`. **Two different answers to the same question in one sprint is the finding.**

`cmd_reship` does not have it. Checked directly rather than inferred: `check_ci_status` and `CI_STATUS_*` appear nowhere in cmd_reship's body — its only guards are the phase check, the is-git-repository check, and the commit-resolves check. cmd_ship calls `check_ci_status` at its line 55 and branches on RED and UNDETERMINABLE. So the two paths currently give different answers to the same question, which is the criterion's own stated finding condition.

REQUIRED: implement it, matching cmd_ship's specificity and its undeterminable-status behaviour rather than deciding that question a second time.

THE REQUIREMENT ITSELF IS RIGHT, and I want that on the record since it came from a question I raised and then explicitly did not push: "a reship ships a commit gate 1 has never seen... exempting it means the least-audited path gets the least mechanical scrutiny." That is a better argument than the one I made in round 1, where I flagged the gap and left it as Master Controller's to decide deliberately. Adding it mid-flight, while a re-audit was already required and therefore free, is the right call and the right moment.

WHAT I AM ACTUALLY FLAGGING is that the handoff described this round as the version change only. Had I taken that at face value and diffed only the code, I would have passed a sprint against a spec I had not re-read, and the new requirement would have shipped unimplemented with a PASS behind it. The fresh-read step is not a formality and this is the second time this sprint it has caught something the handoff did not surface — the first being the uncommitted spec last round.

This is sprint 18's Req 7 in reverse. That rule is about removing a requirement from Requirements and Acceptance Criteria when it is rescoped out, rather than only noting it in Dependencies. The mirror image is adding one to both without the work, and it produces the same result: a spec section that describes work that is not this commit's reality.

================================================================
EVERYTHING ELSE STANDS ON IDENTICAL BYTES
================================================================

The version correction is right and the reasoning behind it is worth recording: `npm publish` retags `latest` to whatever it just published regardless of semver order, the registry's latest is 0.1.27, and shipping 0.1.25 would have moved `latest` backward for every unpinned install. Caught before a ship rather than after, by checking `npm help publish` rather than assuming — the second publish-ordering hazard this project has found that way. package.json is 0.1.28 and the committed spec now says 0.1.28 in the requirement, the QA1 criterion and the LiveQA criterion, so code and spec agree in all three places.

Not re-derived, verified in round 1 against bytes that have not changed: Req 1's seven-case scratch demonstration (bookkeeping/sprint-file/identical-content accepted; four kinds of real code change refused, including a file that did not exist at ship time), the mismatch message naming both differing paths, the helper reuse; Req 2's specificity including the synthetic-step exclusion; Req 3's origin/* precedent argument, which I pushed on four ways and which held.

Re-ran everything anyway rather than carrying results across two commits: ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED; ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED, 181 OK; verify-tarball.sh PASSED, "Installed 0.1.28 (first install)".

================================================================
ON THE COST DEV TEAM STATED
================================================================

Recorded because the self-assessment is accurate and because the record should carry it: this was the sixth instance of a rule this project wrote for itself in sprint 18, and the first where the unrecorded artifact was a gate verdict. Two audits existed on a sprint whose state file was not in git; had it been lost, the record would have shown none.

The observation that it lands on the sprint immediately before the one written to fix it is the useful part, not the irony. Sprint 27's Finding A — nothing commits lifecycle bookkeeping, so it accumulates until someone sweeps it — was written yesterday and demonstrated today by the person who wrote it, knowing the rule and having cited it hours earlier. That is the strongest possible evidence for its Req 1, and it is worth carrying into that sprint's own file as a dated instance rather than leaving it in this handoff: a rule that is known, written down, and recently cited still did not fire, because nothing was watching at the moment the wrong conclusion formed.

RECOMMENDATION

Implement Req 4, then round 3. It will genuinely be short — I have re-read the spec, everything else is verified against unchanged bytes, and I will be checking one function and re-running the suite.

INFORMATIONAL, CARRIED: every allowlist entry other than git and npm remains inferred; the empty-string ownedRepository declaration still falls through silently.

PASS: PASS — round 3. Audited 6d5c2f8, main checkout. Sprint file re-read fresh from the committed copy; `git diff bdd74bc HEAD -- docs/sprints/2-in-progress/sprint-24_*.md` is empty, so the spec is unchanged since round 2 — which is the check that made round 2 not-short, and it is worth doing every time for exactly that reason.

REQ 4 — MET, AND MET TO THE CRITERION'S ACTUAL TEST

The criterion is not "does reship have a CI check" but "does it give the same answer as ship — two different answers to the same question in one sprint is the finding." Extracted both function bodies and compared the CI logic side by side:

    cmd_ship:    ci_status, ci_detail = check_ci_status(shipped_commit)
                 if ci_status == CI_STATUS_RED:            -> die(... "No override.")
                 elif ci_status == CI_STATUS_UNDETERMINABLE: -> warn to stderr, proceed
    cmd_reship:  ci_status, ci_detail = check_ci_status(reshipped_commit)
                 if ci_status == CI_STATUS_RED:            -> die(... "No override.")
                 elif ci_status == CI_STATUS_UNDETERMINABLE: -> warn to stderr, proceed

Same helper, same three branches, same refusal with no override, same warn-and-proceed with the same stated reasoning (a project with no CI must not become unshippable by accident). The only difference is the word "shipped" versus "reshipped" in the messages, which is correct — the message should name the command the operator actually ran.

TWO THINGS BEYOND THE REQUIREMENT, both closing gaps I would otherwise have carried:

  1. The shared helper's own docstring now names BOTH callers and instructs whoever changes its grading
     to keep them consistent — "two call sites giving different answers to the same question is exactly
     the defect Req 4 exists to remove." That converts a one-time fix into a standing constraint on the
     next person, which is the difference between fixing this instance and preventing the next.
  2. The reshipped history event now records the CI verdict (`ci={status}: {detail}`) — and I checked
     cmd_ship does the same, at line 1316 against 1385, identical format. So the two paths agree in the
     durable record as well as in behaviour, not just at the point of decision. Nobody asked for that
     and it is the half that matters six months later.

SCOPE — EXACTLY THE ONE FUNCTION NAMED. Filtered the sprint_lifecycle.py diff for non-comment changes: cmd_reship's new CI branch, its log_event line, and the shared docstring. Nothing else. Three new smoke sections, matching the ship-side ones one for one: red refuses, succeeded-but-no-real-step refuses, undeterminable warns without gating — the same three cases, so the coverage is symmetric rather than nominally present.

ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED; ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED, 181 OK; verify-tarball.sh PASSED, "Installed 0.1.28 (first install)"; package.json 0.1.28, matching the committed spec in all three places it appears.

EVERYTHING FROM ROUNDS 1 AND 2 STANDS, not re-derived: Req 1's seven-case scratch demonstration in both directions and the mismatch message naming the differing paths; Req 2's specificity including the synthetic-step exclusion; Req 3's origin/* precedent argument, which I pushed on four ways; and the 0.1.28 version correction and its reasoning.

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it. /sprint-dev-done 24, then Pipeman ships and publishes 0.1.28, then `verify-publish 24`.

Two notes for Pipeman, because this release changes that role's own tooling underneath it:
  - Both /sprint-ship AND /sprint-reship can now refuse on CI status. If either does, read which of the
    two conditions it names — concluded not-success, or succeeded with no real step — before treating
    it as a tooling problem. That distinction is the whole point of the check.
  - This is the release where 0.1.28 is deliberately not the next number after 0.1.24's original slot.
    `npm publish` retags `latest` unconditionally, so publishing anything below 0.1.27 would move
    `latest` backward for every unpinned install. If the version looks wrong, it is not.

Three rounds. Round 1 audited the build, round 2 caught a requirement added without its implementation, round 3 is the implementation. The thing that made rounds 2 and 3 necessary was not a defect in the code — it was the spec moving after a verdict, twice, and being caught both times by re-reading it rather than by trusting a handoff that said nothing had.
